title: The Offered Hand
passage:
Every guide to the new etiquette ___(1)___ the handshake to the past. Illustrated cards went up in lift lobbies, the nod and the raised palm were drilled into staff at induction, and for a season or two the drill held. ___(2)___ the hand came back. Larkmoor, a workplace consultancy that has watched office greetings each spring since 2016, found last year that four in five first meetings still opened with one — a figure only a little below the one it recorded before anybody had heard of the substitutes. Its fieldworkers still count on clipboards, because nobody has built them anything better.

Nothing about the gesture is easy to defend. It is unhygienic, unequal in force, and clumsy for anyone whose hands are full. To decline one is still to owe a small ___(3)___, which is a strange burden to hang on a greeting, and every alternative on offer is cleaner than it is. Ilse Vandermeer, who has run the Larkmoor survey since its second year, is careful not to claim she knows why the cleaner options lost. What her interviews hold is only what people say the moment does for them.

The moment they describe is seldom ___(4)___: most call it a small test they are glad to have passed, and a few admit to having rehearsed it beforehand. That is not the language of a comfortable ritual but of something with stakes — a half-second in which force, timing and attention are all being read at once, and in which the reading goes both ways. A nod across a room asks nothing and settles nothing; it can be repeated, hedged, or quietly withdrawn. A hand once out has to be met or refused, and either way an answer now exists. Whatever else it is doing, the handshake brings the first half-second of an encounter to a ___(5)___ — and in a working day made largely of unfinished exchanges, that may be the scarcest thing it has left to offer.
— Bernadette Iles, columnist

The frame is 'Every guide to the new etiquette ___ the handshake to the past', and the fixed English idiom for declaring something obsolete is 'consign X to the past': 'consigned' locks. assigned = collocation_misfit (one assigns a task, a room or a value to someone, not a custom 'to the past'; the frame has the right preposition for the idiom but the wrong verb). designed = collocation_misfit (a real -signed verb of the same shape, thematically near 'guide', but 'designed the handshake to the past' is not English). resigned = collocation_misfit (the idiom demands a reflexive object and a different preposition — one is 'resigned to' something, one does not 'resign the handshake to the past'). Only 'consigned' collocates with 'to the past' in this frame.

Connective-logic gap; all four are sentence-initial connective adverbs (connective class matched). The sentence before it closes on the substitutes succeeding — 'for a season or two the drill held' — and the gapped sentence reverses that outcome: 'the hand came back'. Only a contrastive connective carries the reversal, so 'Yet' fits. Thus = wrong_logic (marks a consequence, but the drill holding cannot be the cause of the handshake's return; the two clauses stand against each other, not in sequence). Likewise = wrong_logic (signals a parallel case, and no second, similar case is on the table — the sentence contradicts the one before rather than echoing it). Besides = wrong_logic (adds a further point in the same direction, whereas the gapped sentence turns the paragraph around). Only 'Yet' marks the reversal the paragraph is built on.

Collocation gap; all four are abstract ex-...-ation nouns (POS-uniform and shape-matched). The frame is 'To decline one is still to owe a small ___', and the verb 'owe' takes a narrow set of objects — one owes money, thanks, an apology or an explanation. 'Owe a small explanation' is the locking collocation and it fits the sense the clause goes on to give ('a strange burden to hang on a greeting'). exclamation = collocation_misfit (a cry or an outburst; 'owe an exclamation' does not exist in English). exploration = collocation_misfit (an investigation; nothing is owed by exploring, and the noun does not take 'owe'). expectation = collocation_misfit and sense misfit (one may raise or meet an expectation, but one does not owe one; an expectation is held by the other party, not handed over). Only 'explanation' is idiomatic after 'owe'.

Polarity gap; all four are adjectives and three share the un- prefix, so the set is shape-matched. 'The moment they describe is seldom ___' inverts polarity: whatever fills the gap is what the moment usually is NOT, and the evidence that follows ('a small test they are glad to have passed', 'admit to having rehearsed it') describes unease. The moment is therefore seldom free of unease: 'untroubled' locks. troubled = polarity_mirror (the skimmer matches the negative mood of the evidence to the negative word, but 'seldom troubled' asserts the moment is usually easy, which is exactly what the respondents deny). unrehearsed = surface_word_match plus quantifier_upgrade (it echoes 'rehearsed' in the same sentence, but the text says only 'a few' admit to rehearsing, so 'seldom unrehearsed' — meaning nearly everyone rehearses — upgrades that few into the norm). uneventful = collocation and sense misfit (it grades an episode for incident, not a person's feeling about a greeting, and 'a moment seldom uneventful' answers a question the passage never asks). Only 'untroubled' survives the inversion the frame imposes.

Collocation gap with a shape-matched cl-/c- noun set. The frame is 'the handshake brings the first half-second of an encounter to a ___', and the fixed idiom is 'bring something to a close' — finish it — which is the point the paragraph has been building ('has to be met or refused, and either way an answer now exists'). clause = collocation_misfit (a legal or grammatical unit; 'bring to a clause' is not English, though the legal flavour suits the negotiating imagery). course = collocation_misfit (English has 'in due course' and 'run its course', but 'bring an encounter to a course' does not exist). cause = collocation_misfit (one may bring a cause to court or take up a cause; 'bring a half-second to a cause' is meaningless here). Only 'close' collocates with 'bring ... to a'.
